---
title: "Tributary — Overview"
description: "Problem, architecture, and results in sixty seconds."
---

## The problem

A simulated two-sided marketplace sells personal-loan leads to lenders through
a six-tier sequential waterfall auction. Like most companies that grew fast,
its data grew in pieces: engineering logs auction events to a data lake, sales
operations runs the CRM, and a marketing agency exports campaign data to its
own warehouse. Three silos, three identity schemes, no shared key — so the
questions that matter most (what did this lead sell for? how many distinct
consumers do we actually have? what revenue did marketing drive?) are
unanswerable.

Tributary builds that world deliberately, then fixes it — and because the
world is simulated from a hidden ground truth, every unification claim is
*scored*, not asserted.

## Architecture

```text
             simulation engine (local Python, seeded, --scale dial)
                  │            │            │
          ┌───────▼──┐   ┌─────▼─────┐  ┌───▼──────────┐
          │ AWS S3   │   │ Neon      │  │ BigQuery     │
          │ auction  │   │ Postgres  │  │ marketing    │
          │ lake     │   │ CRM       │  │ exports      │
          └───────┬──┘   └─────┬─────┘  └───┬──────────┘
                  └──────┬─────┴─────┬──────┘
                         ▼           ▼
              DuckDB + dbt + Splink (unification, scored vs. ground truth)
                         │
                         ▼
         wide analytics marts · static dashboards · ML models
```

One seeded command regenerates everything at any scale: 1.5M consumer records,
2.4M leads, 26.4M auction events, and 2.19M marketing messages in about two
and a half minutes at full scale. The simulator is calibrated against three
public datasets (iPinYou bid logs, LendingClub applications, Criteo uplift),
so its distributions are defensible, and the silo fracture injects the
identity pathologies that make unification genuinely hard.

## Results in sixty seconds

| Claim | Number | Where it's proven |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Auction revenue events joinable to a consumer | **95.3%**, up from 0% | [ER scorecard](https://github.com/JordanBeary/tributary/blob/main/er/scorecard.json), [details](silo-problem.qmd) |
| Entity-resolution accuracy vs. hidden ground truth | link F1 **0.879**, dedupe F1 **0.873** | [ER pipeline](https://github.com/JordanBeary/tributary/tree/main/er) |
| Consumer identity: apparent vs. real | 2.40M lead ids → **635,579** consumers (3.8x overcount) | [Identity dashboard](dashboards.qmd) |
| Duplicate spend exposed by unification | **$12.0M** (5.7% of revenue) paid for consumers bought within the prior 30 days | [Auction dashboard](dashboards.qmd) |
| Marketing revenue attribution, previously impossible | **93%** of $209.2M revenue attributed; channel ROAS 0.94x–3.06x | [Attribution dashboard](dashboards.qmd) |
| Total cloud bill for the three-silo deployment | **$0.01** | [Cost engineering](cost.qmd) |
| Warehouse scan cost after partitioning | **10.9x** fewer bytes scanned | [Benchmark receipt](https://github.com/JordanBeary/tributary/blob/main/silos/marketing_bq/benchmark_receipt.json) |

## What's here now, what's next

This first release covers the build through analytics: the silo story,
entity resolution with its scorecard, cost engineering, and six dashboards.
The ML workstream (sale propensity, censored price modeling, reserve-price
optimization, uplift) is trained and evaluated but publishes here only after
its review closes — an ordering chosen deliberately so the site never cites
unratified numbers.

Start with [the silo problem](silo-problem.qmd), or skip to
[how this was built](method.qmd) if the working method is what you came for.
